person.name: Aditya Reddy
person.title: Senior Software Engineer
person.tagline: Senior software engineer. I build and run production systems for companies where downtime has a dollar sign attached to it.

about: Right now I lead observability for a major application rebuild at Northwestern Mutual. The legacy and rebuilt stacks run side by side, and the monitoring has to referee between them fairly or the comparison is worthless. I defined the SLI framework the stakeholders signed off on, and moved measurement to the gateway instead of trusting what each application reports about itself.

Before that I was a core engineer on straight-through processing of insurance applications: 16 Node microservices, 3 React apps, an event-driven architecture on AWS. I took the team's DevSecOps role cause someone had to, and it turned out I liked the pipelines as much as the product. PagerDuty on-call too. You should carry the pager for what you build though.
Nine years in software, seven of them building and operating production web systems in the US, across financial services, healthcare and retail supply chain.

story.heading: Started in the pixels.
story.text: Years of shipping interfaces people actually touch. The label that stuck at work is frontend guru, though these days the pixels are only half the job.

story.heading: Then the stack underneath.
story.text: Backend, cloud, pipelines, security. Each layer cause the one above it kept breaking on something I couldn't see yet.

story.heading: Averages hide the users who are waiting.
story.text: The distribution has a tail, and the tail is where the experience actually happens. p95 says someone is hurting. p99 says who.

story.heading: One keystroke. 300 re-renders.
story.text: A form-heavy enterprise app cloned its whole state tree on every keystroke. Each of those re-renders is a component doing pointless work.

story.heading: Rewrite the state layer and it's one.
story.text: Instrumented numbers, not an estimate. INP 426ms → 268ms

story.heading: Now the platform under all of it.
story.text: Kubernetes, Vault, Terraform, the release trains. I run what I build, and I carry the pager for it.

story.heading: Faster in the field.
story.text: A controlled experiment proved which change did it. Making it fast is half the job. Proving why is the half people skip.

points: Observability lead for an enterprise application rebuild spanning 4 backend services, 16 user interfaces and 2 databases. SLI design, gateway-level measurement, distributed tracing, release trains, and the CI/CD and security scanning the team ships through.

Core engineer on straight-through processing of underwriting applications. Converted the platform to a multi-case, event-driven design on AWS SQS and SNS, provisioned the messaging infrastructure in Terraform, and shipped reverse approval and decline handling end to end.

Consulting engineer with enterprise clients in healthcare distribution and retail supply chain. React, Redux and Java Spring Boot on an enterprise reporting platform, D3 dashboard visualizations, and a home delivery scheduling platform.
Graduate teaching assistant for Data Visualizations along the way, teaching Tableau, Power BI, SAP Lumira and Excel to graduate students.

Front end on customer-facing web applications, then across the stack: Node.js REST endpoints against SQL Server, and early container work with Docker, Ansible and Kubernetes when that was still a strange thing for a Hyderabad product team to be doing.

projects.name: Desk Studio
projects.summary: A design studio inside the coding agent you already use. Ask for a launch card or a brand kit in plain words, and a small team of model desks makes it, scores it and signs it off.
highlights: A Claude Code plugin, and one npx command for Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Windsurf and OpenCode.
Each job is routed by cost: three roughs on Sonnet, the pick on Opus, polish on Haiku, then a proof step with no model at all.
Every job leaves a note with who did what, the scores and the cost. A chart costs under a dollar, a full brand kit about ten.
Runs on your machine through the CLI you're already signed in to.
The studio designed its own brand kit, which is either a good sign or a conflict of interest.

projects.name: react-inp-blame
projects.summary: When a click, tap or key press in your React app is slow, this names the component or the handler behind it and says where the time went.
highlights: Which React component made this interaction slow. Joins Event Timing and Long Animation Frames to the React fiber tree.
Writes a plain-language verdict for each slow click, tap or key press, and adds tracks to Chrome's Performance panel.
Setups for Next.js 14.2 or later and Vite, plus React Router, Remix, TanStack Start and Astro.
On four open-source apps, built with and without it, INP did not move on any of them.
Everything in the demo is slow on purpose, which is the only time I will ever say that about my code.

projects.summary: The scroll film that used to be the front page, now at /about-me. Static, no build step, one HTML file.
highlights: Served by GitHub Pages from main at adityareddy.dev.

articles.title: The pagehide listener that never ran
articles.summary: I removed a pagehide listener that never ran during navigation. Moving it to window could have made logs flush too early and miss final web-vitals records.

articles.title: What broke when I moved Grafana Faro to OpenTelemetry JS 3.0
articles.summary: While preparing Grafana Faro's OpenTelemetry JS 3.0 upgrade, I found a blocked deep import and tests running the Node build. Disabled XHR instrumentation was still creating spans too.

articles.title: Why your INP can fall after one more click
articles.summary: A fast click can lower a page's INP without fixing its slowest interaction. I explain what changes at interaction 50, and why a late observer can miss earlier fast events.

articles.title: How one Desk Studio job gets from roughs to sign-off
articles.summary: The studio's own launch card, followed from three roughs through the pick, three polish rounds, proof and sign-off, with the saved scores and what it cost.

articles.title: Why the OpenTelemetry browser SDK wouldn't start on Safari 17
articles.summary: One call to URL.parse kept the SDK from starting on Safari 17 and on Chrome and Firefox older than 126. The fix, how I tested it without an old browser, and why lint let it through.
